standard.title: Environmental world views
standard.description: the environmental world views of people and their implications for environmental management
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain conflicting stakeholder perspectives on sustainability (AC9HG10K01) and understand human-induced environmental change types. They have engaged with interconnections between human activity and environments (AC9HG9K02, AC9HG9K08) and understand that different people have different relationships to place.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students discuss the influence of people's environmental world views (human-centred and earth-centred) regarding environmental management and explain how world views shape choices of management methods.

nodes.label: Human-centred and earth-centred world views
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between human-centred (anthropocentric) and earth-centred (ecocentric) environmental world views and explain what each implies about the relationship between humans and the environment.
nodes.minimum_width: Define both world view types and describe one management approach associated with each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the philosophical basis and practical implications of human-centred and earth-centred world views; link each to concrete management approaches such as resource extraction vs conservation, economic development vs protected areas.
wider: Investigate intermediate world views such as stewardship ethics or biocentric ethics that complicate the binary, evaluating how each positions human responsibility
Examine how legal frameworks in different countries encode world views — for example, rights of nature legislation in Ecuador or New Zealand vs resource-rights regimes
Compare how Indigenous world views differ from both human-centred and earth-centred Western frameworks, particularly regarding relational ontologies
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish these world views cannot explain why different stakeholders choose different management methods in K04, nor can they discuss whether environmental change is 'necessarily a problem' — a question whose answer depends entirely on one's world view.

response_modes.reason: The human-centred/earth-centred distinction is conceptually slippery — students often assume everyone shares their own world view. Use explicit comparison frameworks (value source, moral standing of nature, justification for management) to make the distinction concrete before applying it.

success_criteria: Students define both human-centred and earth-centred world views using correct terminology
Students identify at least one management approach associated with each world view and explain the connection

nodes.label: World views and causes of environmental issues
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare differences in people's views about the causes of an environmental issue, explaining how world view shapes the identification of causes.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two different perspectives on the causes of one environmental issue, tracing how each perspective reflects a different world view.
nodes.typical_width: For at least one environmental issue of personal, national and global importance, compare perspectives from human-centred and earth-centred stakeholders; explain how each world view leads to a different identification of causes and responsible parties.
wider: Analyse media coverage of a single environmental issue from outlets reflecting different world views, identifying how framing choices (headline, quoted sources, language) encode particular world views
Investigate how scientific consensus on an environmental issue (e.g. climate attribution) intersects with or conflicts with different world view frameworks
Compare how communities in different countries assign cause and responsibility for the same global environmental issue based on historical, economic and cultural factors

response_modes.reason: Analysing cause attribution across multiple issues and stakeholder groups prevents students from applying the world view framework mechanically to a single case.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cause attribution is the most contested aspect of environmental management — examining the same issue through multiple world view lenses deepens students' critical literacy and prepares them for the evaluation demands of K04.
success_criteria: Students explain how two stakeholders with different world views identify different causes for the same environmental issue
Students use the terms 'human-centred' and 'earth-centred' correctly when analysing cause attribution

nodes.label: World views and management choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss whether environmental change is necessarily a problem and explain how people's world views shape their choices of management methods.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how at least one world view leads to a specific management choice, and discuss whether all stakeholders view the change as a problem requiring management.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss multiple management methods (environmental, economic, regulatory, community-based) in terms of the world views they reflect; explain why not all stakeholders agree that a given change is a problem requiring intervention.
wider: Evaluate a specific environmental management decision at national or international scale — identifying which world views are reflected in the chosen strategy and which are marginalised
Investigate cases where communities chose not to manage or reverse an environmental change, examining the world view basis for that choice
Compare how different cultural or religious traditions within a single country produce divergent views on whether and how to manage a specific environmental change

response_modes.reason: This node integrates world view identification, cause attribution and management choice into a coherent explanatory chain. Students need to coordinate all three moves — a teacher signal to make the connections explicit rather than treating each move as separate.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The integration of world view into management choice analysis is the core analytical skill for K04. Students who have explored multiple management decisions through the world view lens develop a richer evaluative repertoire.
success_criteria: Students explain how a specific world view leads to a specific management approach (or non-intervention) using correct terminology
Students discuss, with evidence, why people holding different world views may disagree on whether an environmental change requires management
